title: Navigation for a fintech product
metaTitle: Fintech product website navigation that matches jobs
excerpt: Fintech navigation should label the jobs a buyer already has words for, and keep one path that starts an account or a sales conversation.
alt: Smooth overlapping waves of blue, violet, and warm orange, distinct bands a person can follow, for a navigation scheme that should separate jobs instead of blending them.
caption: Overlapping bands of blue, violet, and orange. Labels should stay this distinct. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should be in a fintech site's main navigation?
faqs.answer: Put the product, the price shape, the jobs you do, proof, and one path to start an account or talk to sales. Use words the buyer already says. Leave departments, blog categories, and legal documents out of the header. Those can live in the footer, where someone looks when they already mean to find them.

faqs.question: How many items belong in the header?
faqs.answer: Few enough that a person can read them on a phone without opening a puzzle. Five or six clear labels is a practical ceiling for most money products. A mega-menu of every feature hides the path. If a label needs a paragraph in the menu, it is a page, not a nav item.

faqs.question: Should Login and Open account both be in the nav?
faqs.answer: Yes, if both are real and they look different. Login is for people who already have access, and opening an account or talking to sales is for people who do not. Give the new-customer path the stronger visual weight, with login as a quiet text link. Do not make returning users hunt, and do not make new buyers think the only action is to sign in.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results
How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Fintech product website navigation is a map of jobs, not a list of departments. A buyer who may trust you with money should see labels they already use, and one path that starts an account or a sales conversation.

If the header reads like an org chart, the buyer has to translate before they can move. Translation is a tax. On a money decision, they will not pay it for long.

## Jobs, not the org chart

Write the labels from the buyer's tasks. Product. Pricing. Payouts, or whatever the job is called in their mouth. Proof. A way to start. Those are destinations. "Solutions," "Company," "Resources," and "Platform" are folders your team made for itself.

Google's guidance on title links prefers titles that describe the page, stay concise, and avoid vague language. Navigation is the same promise, one step earlier. The label is the title the visitor sees before the page title. If the label is "Solutions" and the page is about seller payouts, you have trained both the visitor and the search result to be confused. Name the payouts.

Nielsen Norman Group found that people often leave a page in the first 10 to 20 seconds, and that they read only about a quarter of the text on pages they do open. Navigation has to survive that impatience. A buyer should be able to choose a destination without reading a menu essay. If a dropdown needs an introductory paragraph, the information architecture is doing the writing's job. Fix the labels.

Test the map by covering the logo and reading only the header. Could a new buyer tell what to tap to see the product, the price shape, and the way in? If they would have to open three menus to answer, the header is a filing system.

## Words the buyer already uses

Collect ten phrases from sales calls and support tickets before you name the nav. The words will be plainer than the brand workshop. "Fees." "Where is my payout." "Who holds the money." "Open an account." Use those words in the header even if the brand line is more poetic. Poetry can live in a sentence. The nav is a sign.

Keep one name per job across the site. If the homepage says "payouts," the nav should not say "disbursements" unless you have a one-line reason. Synonyms feel sophisticated inside a writing review. They feel like lost pages to a person in a hurry.

Avoid internal product code names in the header. A code name is fine on a page for current customers. A prospect should not have to learn it to find pricing. Put the code name in the product page body if engineers and returning users search for it. The label stays in the buyer's language.

Legal and regulatory words belong where the buyer expects the fact, not as a top-level mood. "Trust" as a nav item usually hides a pile of policies. Name the policy they might want: security, licenses, funds. A buyer looking for who holds the money will not guess that the answer is under Trust.

## One path that starts the relationship

One item in the header is the action. Open an account, or talk to sales. Style it as the action, and do not let a second action compete at the same weight. Login can sit beside it as a quieter link. Documentation can sit in the footer or in a product menu for people who already intend to build.

The action label must match the button on the homepage and the pricing page. A buyer who taps "Talk to sales" should land on a page that talks about that conversation, not a general contact form with a subject dropdown. If you have two real entry paths, self-serve and sales, the nav can expose both only when the words say who each is for. "Start" and "Demo" do not say that. "Open an account" and "Talk to sales" do.

Do not put the action only inside a menu. On a phone, the path should be visible without a tap, or available on the first tap of the menu with no scrolling. Hiding the account button inside a list of blog categories is how a careful buyer gives up and emails a person they already know instead.

If the product is login-walled, the marketing nav and the app nav are different maps. Do not mix "Settings" and "Pricing" in one bar. A prospect and a signed-in operator are having different days. Show the map that matches the day.

## What belongs in the header

A header for this kind of product can stay small:

- The product, in the buyer's name for it.
- Pricing, meaning the shape of the price.
- The one or two jobs you want recognized, if they are not obvious from the product label.
- Proof, if you have a story with a decision, not a logo dump.
- The action: account or sales.
- A quiet login.

That list is already plenty. Features that matter belong on the product page, grouped under the job. A menu that lists every API object is a documentation site leaking into the marketing header. Link to docs once, from the footer or from the product page, for the person who asked.

Dropdowns are justified when a buyer must choose among real jobs. Payouts versus issuing, if those are different hires. They are not justified as a place to park pages you do not want to delete. If a dropdown item gets no traffic and no sales mentions, it is a candidate for the footer or for removal.

Order the items in the order of a first visit. Product, then price, then proof, then the action. Company news does not belong between product and pricing. A buyer should not have to pass your press page to find the fee.

## What belongs in the footer

The footer is for people who are looking on purpose. Legal, privacy, licenses, status, security details, careers, a postal address if you publish one, and a way to reach support that is different from sales. Label support as support. A buyer with a failed payout should not land in a sales queue because the footer said "Contact."

Repeat the main jobs in the footer in the same words as the header. Footers are how people recover when the header was too clever. Do not invent a second vocabulary down there. Do not add a column of keyword pages that exist only to rank. Google's title guidance is a reminder that every linked page should be a real subject. A column called "Resources" full of near-duplicates is a smell, in the nav and in the index.

Include the accountable entity where a money buyer looks for it. The legal name, the country, and a pointer to the license or the partner, in ordinary type. A footer that is only a newsletter form has used the one place cautious people scroll to, and spent it on a list.

## Mobile navigation is the real navigation

Design the small screen first. The header that looked spacious on a desktop mock will collapse into an icon. Decide, before that happens, which two things remain visible: the wordmark and the action. Everything else can live behind the menu if the menu is a short list of the same jobs, in the same order.

Tap targets need to be easy to hit with a thumb, and the action should not sit under a floating chat button. The control has to work, and it needs a name a person can understand. "Menu" is understandable. A mystery icon with no name is not. Give the button an accessible name.

Do not auto-advance carousels inside the open menu. Do not load the menu with promotional cards. A person opened it to go somewhere. Let them go. Close the menu when they choose, and make sure the focus lands on the new page's heading, not back on the footer of the page they left.

Hanabi builds these headers in the same Next.js site as the pages, so the nav is not a plugin with a different set of words. [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works) shows how public projects keep a small set of destinations. The useful habit is the edit: fewer labels, each one a job.

## A label review you can run in an hour

Print the header, or write it in a single column. For each label, answer three questions. What job does this buyer think this is? What page will actually open? What would we remove if we had to lose two items? If the first two answers diverge, rename or merge. If you cannot bear to lose anything, you do not have a map yet. You have a wishlist.

Read the labels to someone who has never seen the deck. Ask them where they would tap to find out who holds funds, what the fee looks like, and how to start. Note the words they use when they get it wrong. Those words are your next draft.

Then check the logged-in product, the docs, and the marketing site side by side. The noun for the main job should match. A payout in the marketing nav that is called a transfer in the product and a disbursement in the docs is three products. Pick one and change the others on a schedule you can finish. Navigation is a promise that the building is labeled the same way on every floor.

Pictures are the next place labels go wrong, because a photograph can argue something the nav just clarified. [Photography direction for a fintech product](/blog/photography-direction-for-a-fintech-product) is about making the pictures show the product and the people, instead of a mood of trust.
